synthesis.topic: Capicúa: definition, doubles, equal ends, bonus amount, domino only (not tranque)
synthesis.consensus: Capicúa is a bonus on the way a hand ends by domino. A domino means a player plays his last tile and his hand is empty. Test it on the two open end values L and R just before that final play, and on the final tile (a,b). It is capicúa only when all three hold. (1) The play empties the player's hand. It never applies to a tranque, because in a tranque nobody goes out. (2) The tile is not a double (a != b). (3) The tile could legally go on either end: it matches L and it matches R. When L != R, this means {a,b} = {L,R}, for example ends 3 and 5 with last tile 3-5. The end the player actually picks does not matter. Only whether the tile fits both ends matters. For the owner's example (ends 2 and 2, last tile 2-2), the answer is NOT capicúa, because the tile is a double. Every Dominican source that mentions doubles excludes them. The case of ends 5 and 5 with last tile 5-6 (L == R, a non-double that contains L) is disputed and unresolved. The literal "fits both ends" wording (Wikipedia, DR1, ASALE) would count it. FichaFlow explicitly does not. No tournament rule decides it. The bonus is 25 points in most sources: DR1, Santiago 2019 tournament, El Día "Capicúa, 25", dominoarteociencia, and a Dominican scorekeeper app. 30 is the second common value (La Guáyiga 2025 tournament). Wikipedia says 25 or 30 by table rules. The bonus goes to the side of the player who goes out, on top of the normal domino hand points (DR1: "another 25 points"; La Mesa: added to the normal hand points). It is a patio and municipal-tournament bonus only. Federation play has no capicúa. Implementation sketch: isCapicua = handEmptied && a != b && fits(L) && fits(R), where fits(x) = (a == x || b == x). The L == R non-double case is a flag the owner decides (FichaFlow-strict would require L != R). capicuaBonus is configurable: default 25, option 30.
synthesis.federationView: Not covered by the federations. I read the FID rulebooks (2015 via pagat.com, 2024 via fidomino.org) and the FEMUNDO 2025 rulebook (femundo.org/reglamento.html). None of them has a capicúa bonus, and none has a pase de salida or pase corrido bonus. A hand scores only the tiles left, and a match is won only by hand points reaching the target. The Federación Dominicana de Dominó (Fededodo) has no published rulebook that anyone could find. Spanish Wikipedia lists capicúa only under the informal (patio) mode, not under the Dominican "regla general" mode. Two Dominican municipal tournaments do use it. The Copa Alcaldía de Santiago 2019 rules say "LA CAPICUA SON 25 TANTOS". The La Guáyiga 2025 rules say "Capicúa: +30 pts." Neither tournament defines capicúa or says anything about doubles. Outside the DR, a Chicago tournament that uses Puerto Rican style excludes doubles and pays 50.

synthesis.topic: pases: pass bonuses (pase de salida, pase corrido / paso redondo, single pass), amounts, recipients, 1v1 vs parejas, and whether a pass bonus can win the game
synthesis.consensus:
Informal (patio) Dominican parejas play has exactly two pass bonuses. Each bonus goes to the TEAM of the player whose tile caused the pass. Play order is to the right (counter-clockwise).

(1) PASE DE SALIDA (also called puntos de salida or paso a la salida). It applies only to the first tile of a hand. Trigger: the player to the opener's right (the next seat) cannot play on the opening tile. Result: the opener's team scores the bonus. Cancellation: if the next player after that (the opener's partner) also cannot play, the bonus is void (Wikipedia es, DR1 article, DR1 forum 1999). Value: 25 is the most common number (Santiago 2019 tournament, dominoarteociencia, FichaFlow default, the Domino Apunte scorekeeper). Other values: 25 or 30 (Wikipedia, "depending on the rules"), 10 in games to 200/250 and 25 in games to 500 (DR1), 10 (DR1 forum 2009, Boarden app), 30 (a Republica domino user review).

(2) PASE CORRIDO / PASO REDONDO. Trigger: a player places a tile, then all three other players (both opponents AND the partner) pass in turn, and the turn comes back to that player. Result: that player's team scores 25 (DR1, dominoarteociencia, FichaFlow) or 25 or 30 (Wikipedia). The same player then plays again. DR1 says there is no limit per hand, so the bonus can repeat. It is not awarded when the table is locked (tranque), because a locked hand ends and nobody plays again (FichaFlow).

(3) ANY OTHER PASS scores nothing. This includes a single opponent passing mid-hand, or two players passing and the third one playing. DR1 is explicit that only the salida and the corrido pay.

Implementation sketch: after the opening tile, set salidaPending = true when seat+1 passes. Award it to the opener's team if seat+2 plays; void it if seat+2 passes. For the corrido, keep lastPlacer and a count of consecutive passes. When passes reach 3, the turn is back at lastPlacer, and lastPlacer holds a legal tile (so this is not a tranque), credit the corrido to lastPlacer's team and reset the count.

1v1: no Dominican source defines pass bonuses for 1v1. FichaFlow says the paso redondo does not exist at a two-player table. My own reasoning, not from a source: with the standard 1v1 rules (7 tiles each, draw from the pile), a player who cannot play draws, so a real pass only happens once the pile is empty. A pase de salida can then never happen, because the pile holds 14 tiles on the first turn.

TARGET: no Dominican source says whether a pass bonus can take a team to or past the target. The Dominican wording is that the game ends when a pair "alcanza o supera" (reaches or passes) the target, with no written exception for bonuses. Read literally, a bonus that reaches the target ends the game, but no source addresses this case directly.
synthesis.federationView:
Federation rulebooks: FID (2015 via pagat, 2024 via fidomino.org) and FEMUNDO 2025 (the world body that Fededodo sends the Dominican team to) have NO pass bonuses of any kind, and no capicua bonus. A hand scores only the tiles left in hand. A match is won only when hand points reach the target (200). FEMUNDO Art. 13 treats a paso corrido only as the same player playing again, not as a move out of turn. FID Art. 80 says that saying "paso" counts as making a move. Pase con ficha (passing while holding a playable tile) costs 40% of the target plus a yellow card (FEMUNDO Art. 16, FID Art. 81). FEMUNDO adds that doing it on purpose loses the match 0-200. The researchers found no published rulebook from the Dominican federation (Fededodo / FEDOMDOM).

Dominican municipal tournaments: the Santiago 2019 Copa Alcaldia rules pay 25 for the pase de salida, pay 0 for the paso corrido, and treat pase con ficha as a 100-point swing (-50 to the offending pair, +50 to the other pair) followed by a reshuffle. The La Guayiga 2025 rules list "Paso corrido: +30 pts al equipo contrario" among their penalty lines. The wording is ambiguous, but most likely it means the team opposite the passers, which is the team of the player who caused the corrido. The same rules give +30 to the other team for pase con ficha. Neither tournament mentions whether bonuses can win the game or are capped at the target.

Summary: in federation play the question does not arise, because no bonuses exist. The bonuses are a patio and municipal-tournament feature.

synthesis.ownerView:
Not covered by any Dominican source, and it gets only weak support from elsewhere. The owner's amounts (25 or 30) match the Wikipedia patio values and the La Guayiga 30. The owner's two limits are: (a) a bonus counts only if it does not take the team past the target, and (b) a game can be won only by winning a round. No Dominican media, reference, forum, or tournament source states either limit. The researchers searched for this point specifically and found nothing Dominican.

The only written source for (a) plus (b) is the Boarden app, which says bonuses are capped and a team must win a hand to cross the target. Boarden does not say whether 'capped' means the bonus is dropped or cut down to the target minus 1. The closest traditional rule is the Cuban 'no caben' rule. That rule is Cuban, optional, and applies to all points, not only bonuses.

The Dominican wording that does exist leans slightly against the owner. Wikipedia RD says the game ends when a pair reaches or passes ('alcanza o supera') the target, with no exception, but it does not discuss bonuses. Federation rules (FID, FEMUNDO) make (b) true only because they have no bonuses at all. So they give no support to a cap as a Dominican custom.

Verdict: treat the rule as a house rule that the owner chooses and states in the app's rules text. It is not a documented Dominican rule, and it is also not contradicted by any source that addresses the case. Note: the owner's two statements together imply that a bonus which lands a team exactly ON the target also must not end the game. The owner should confirm that edge.

The Dominican patio section gives salida and corrido at 25 or 30 with the partner cancel, and pase con ficha penalties. It is also the source of the 'alcanza o supera' game-end wording, which has no exception for bonuses.
The Santiago 2019 municipal tournament rules: pase de salida 25, paso corrido worth 0, pase con ficha a 100-point swing. This is the strongest Dominican tournament evidence.
The La Guayiga 2025 municipal tournament rules: paso corrido +30 with ambiguous direction, pase con ficha +30 to the other team.
FEMUNDO 2025 (Art. 13, 16): no pass bonuses, paso corrido means only that the same player plays again, pase con ficha costs 40% of the target. It is the world body for the Dominican national team.
The FID 2024 rulebook: no bonuses, and matches are won only by hand points. This confirms the federation baseline.

openQuestions: Can a pass bonus win the game? No Dominican source addresses this. The owner must choose between the literal 'reaches or passes the target ends the game' reading and a cap (the Boarden / owner rule), and state the choice in the rules text.

If the owner keeps the cap: is the bonus dropped entirely, or cut down to stop at the target minus 1? And does a bonus that lands a team exactly on the target count? The owner's two statements imply that it must not end the game.

Timing: is the bonus credited the moment it happens, or at the end of the hand? DR1 reads as immediate. Boarden's opener-pass wording ('in a hand where the winner opened') suggests that some implementations award it only at the end, or only when the opener's team wins the hand.

If the opener's next opponent passes, the partner passes (which voids the salida), and the fourth player also passes, is that a pase corrido for the opener? The definitions imply yes, but no source addresses the case.
La Guayiga's 'Paso corrido: +30 pts al equipo contrario': which team receives it? The most likely reading is the team of the player who caused it, but the wording is ambiguous.

With draw-from-pile rules a salida pass cannot happen. A 10-tile no-draw variant (Wikipedia) could produce one, and its bonus rules are undocumented.

Which default value: 25 (the most common number) or 30 for both bonuses? DR1 also ties the salida value to the target (10 for 200/250, 25 for 500). The owner should confirm the app's value for each game target.

check.correctedConsensus:
The consensus holds in substance, with four corrections.

1. Two bonuses, verified in the pages I opened. (a) Pase de salida: the next player cannot play on the opening tile. Wikipedia es gives 25 or 30 and voids the bonus if the opener's partner also cannot play. The DR1 forum (1999) gives 25 "providing your partner can play". dominoarteociencia says these plays are "normalmente" 25. The Santiago 2019 tournament gives 25. (b) Pase corrido / redondo: the other three players pass. Wikipedia gives 25 or 30, dominoarteociencia 25 and the DR1 forum 25. Santiago 2019 pays 0 for it. So "exactly two bonuses" describes patio play, not every tournament.

2. Default value: at a 200-point target, both Santiago 2019 (played "a los 200 tantos") and the DR1 forum (play to 200) pay 25 for the salida. The DR1 article's figure of 10 for games to 200/250 is the minority value. 25 is the better-supported default for both bonuses.

3. Not verified in this check: the DR1 article was blocked (web.archive.org). These claims still rest on it alone: salida 10 vs 25 by target, "no limit per hand", and the explicit statement that only salida and corrido pay. The DR1 forum names no other pass bonus, which is consistent with the article. The rule of play to the right and the FichaFlow tranque exclusion were also not checked.

4. Target: Wikipedia says the game ends when a pair "alcanza o supera 100 o 200 puntos". It makes no exception for bonuses and never discusses them. None of the four Dominican sources I opened says whether a pass bonus can win the game. Wikipedia credits the salida to "al jugador que salió". In parejas that means the pair's score.

The 1v1 reasoning and the implementation sketch are unchanged. The sources I opened do not address 1v1.

synthesis.consensus:
Lock detection: the hand ends in a tranque when no player can legally play. In 2v2 all 28 tiles are dealt, so this happens only right after a tile placement that leaves both open ends on the same number N with all 7 tiles containing N on the board (FID Art. 56; the arXiv paper; DR1: all tiles of the needed suits are played). Check after every placement that no hand holds a tile that matches either end. Do not wait for four passes. The blocker is the player who placed that last tile (DR1 "executed the tranque", FichaFlow "placed the blocking tile").

Comparison (Dominican informal/patio rule; this is the most common Dominican-specific statement and the rule in two municipal tournaments): the blocker compares only with "el de abajo". That is the next player in turn order, who sits to his right because Dominican play goes counter-clockwise. In 2v2 this seat, (blocker + 1) mod 4 in turn order, is always an opponent. In 1v1 it is the only opponent. Compare pip totals (the sum of both halves of every tile left in each hand), never tile counts. The lower total wins, and the hand goes to that player's pair. The blocker's partner and the fourth player do not affect who wins.

Points: the winning pair scores the pips left in all four hands, including the winners' own tiles (Wikipedia patio per the research notes, Santiago 2019, FichaFlow worked example 8+11+7+14=40; FID and FEMUNDO also count all four hands in pair mode). DR1's wording ("points in his opponent's hands") and the Wikipedia regla general (per the notes) give the opponents' pips only. A programmer must choose between these two options.

Tie (equal totals): the sources give no single rule. Dominican-specific sources give the hand to the pair of the player who placed the first tile of the hand, and that pair scores (DR1, Wikipedia regla general, La Mesa). Tournaments and federations score nothing and give the lead to the next opener in rotation (Santiago 2019 also reshuffles; FID, FEMUNDO, USA Domino Federation). FichaFlow gives the tie to the blocker.

Next opener: on a tie under the Wikipedia regla general, the pair that opened wins and opens again. Under tournament and federation rules, the next player in the rotation opens (FID and FEMUNDO rotate to the right). For a tranque that someone wins, no source in the file says who opens next.
synthesis.federationView:
No Dominican federation rulebook was found. Fededodo (Federación Dominicana de Dominó) sends its national team to the FEMUNDO world championship but publishes no rules online. Researchers found no FEDOMDOM rulebook either, and one site that names it looked unreliable.

FID (2015, 2021 English, and 2024 editions, Arts. 56-58): a tranca happens when a player places the seventh and last tile of a suit and both ends then show that suit. The pair with fewer points in unplayed tiles wins and scores the unplayed tiles of both pairs. On equal points the tranca is a draw: a zero is recorded for the pair that made the tranca, and the opener rotation continues to the right.

FEMUNDO 2025 (Art. 6): tranques are pair against pair. The winner scores the points of all 4 players. On a tie the points do not count and the opener rotation continues. Art. 11 allows 1 minute to think when a player locks the game or is forced to feed the lock (bandeo).

USA Domino Federation: "Todo tranque será en pareja" (every tranque is by pairs). The pair with fewer tantos wins. On a tie nobody wins and the rotation continues.

Dominican municipal tournaments: La Guáyiga 2025 says "Se tranca con el jugador de abajo" (the blocker against the next player). Santiago 2019 rule 6 says "EL TRANQUE ES CON EL DE ABAJO", but rule 12 of the same sheet says "con todos, pareja con pareja". That is a contradiction inside one rulebook. Santiago scores a tie as no points, reshuffles, and the next player in rotation opens.

No federation or tournament source compares tile counts.

synthesis.ownerView: Supported for Dominican informal (patio) play, and not the only Dominican rule. These are DR1, the Wikipedia (es) patio rule, OurPastimes, FichaFlow, and two municipal tournaments (La Guáyiga 2025; Santiago 2019 rule 6). check.correctedConsensus:
The core rules hold against the 3 sources I could open (Wikipedia es, FichaFlow, FID 2024). DR1 did not load, so every claim that rests only on DR1 is unverified. Five corrections follow.

Lock detection (unchanged, verified): FID Art. 56 defines the tranca as the placement of the seventh and last tile of a suit when both ends then show that suit. In 2v2 with all 28 tiles dealt, a parity argument confirms that "no one can play" is equivalent to this condition. Check after every placement. Do not wait for passes. Edge case to add: if the locking tile is also the player's last tile, the hand ends as a dominada (FID Art. 55), not a tranque. The blocker is the player who placed the locking tile (FichaFlow: the player "who placed the blocking tile"; FID: the pair that "hubiere ejecutado el cierre o tranca").

Comparison, correction 1: remove "the most common Dominican-specific statement". Wikipedia (es) labels pair against pair as the Dominican "regla general" and the blocker-vs-right-opponent rule as the "regla de patio". Counted by Dominican-specific sources, the two rules have about equal support. Federations (FID Art. 58) use pair against pair. The app should offer both modes. Pair mode: each pair sums both partners' pips, and the lower pair total wins. Patio mode (Wikipedia: "compara solo sus fichas con el oponente de la derecha"; FichaFlow: "the next player"): the blocker compares his pip total only with the next player in turn order, (blocker + 1) mod 4, who is always an opponent. The lower total wins for that player's pair. Always compare pips, never tile counts (verified in all three sources).

Points (verified): Patio mode scores all four hands (Wikipedia patio: "se suman los puntos de todas las fichas restantes"; FichaFlow example 8+11+7+14=40). FID Art. 58 pair mode also scores all unplayed tiles of both pairs. Wikipedia regla general scores only the losing pair's pips. The owner must choose between all four hands and the losing side only. Correction 2: the claim that FichaFlow mentions tables that pay only the difference was not found on the page.

Tie, correction 3: each tie rule belongs to a specific mode. Wikipedia gives "the opening pair wins and opens next" for the regla general (pair mode) only, and gives no tie rule for patio mode. FichaFlow (patio-style): "a tie favors the blocker". FID Art. 58 (pair mode): a draw, with a zero recorded for the pair that made the tranca. The DR1 and La Mesa tie claims are unverified here.

Next opener, correction 4: the claim "no source says who opens next after a tranque that someone wins" is too strong. FID rotates the opener every hand ("La próxima mano sale el atleta a la derecha", Art. 76 context), so under federation rules the next player to the right opens after any tranque, won or tied. Correction 5: for informal Dominican play, no source I opened states who opens after a won tranque. This is still an open decision for the owner.

synthesis.topic: Scoring: which hands count when a player goes out, game targets, whether a team can win only by winning a hand, and reaching the target mid-hand
synthesis.consensus: Scoring happens per hand (mano). Hand points go only to the pair that wins the hand, and they equal the pips (tantos) on the unplayed tiles. Dominican sources give two ways to count those tiles when a player goes out (dominada). Neither has a clear majority. (A) Opponents only: sum the two opposing hands. This is the "regla general" in Wikipedia es, DR1 for games to 200 or 250, Acento, Acercate a RD and the Tranca code. (B) All unplayed tiles: sum the opponents' hands plus the partner's hand (the winner's own hand is empty). This is the only Dominican tournament rule found (Santiago 2019: "se cuenta todas las fichas"), DR1 for games to 500, Wikipedia patio play, La Mesa and Boarden. FID and FEMUNDO also count all tiles. Implement the count as a table setting: countPartner: boolean. The game target is a table agreement. 200 is the most cited value (tournaments, all federations, DR1, FichaFlow, La Mesa, forums), and 100 is the common casual value (Acento "hasta un ciento", Wikipedia, Boarden). 150, 250, 500 and 300 also appear. Win check: after each hand is scored, a pair wins when its running total is >= target ("alcanza o supera"; reaching the target exactly is enough). The overshoot is kept and not capped (El Dia reports a 210-180 final). Every source that shows a check does it after the hand is scored (Tranca checks at the end of each hand). No Dominican source describes a win in the middle of a hand. No Dominican source says a team can win only by winning a hand. No Dominican source says whether a mid-hand bonus (pase de salida, paso corrido) that reaches the target ends the game. In 1v1 the partner question does not apply.
synthesis.federationView: FID (Reglamento 2015 and 2024, Art. 57; 2021 English edition): on a dominada, the winning pair scores every unplayed tile in the hand, its partner's tiles included. FID Arts. 61-62: the match goes to the pair that first reaches the preset target by capturing points in hands. The target is 200 at world championships (300 in exceptional cases), with a time limit of 40 minutes (2015) or 35 minutes (2024), and a match cannot end in a tie. FEMUNDO 2025 (Art. 6), which the Dominican federation Fededodo attends: each dominada scores the points of the 3 players still holding tiles, and matches run to 200 tantos or 40 minutes, whichever comes first. USA Domino Federation: 200 tantos or 35 minutes (its counting basis is not in the claim file). None of these rulebooks has capicua or pass bonuses, so every point comes from hand results, and in federation play a pair can reach the target only by winning hands (a dominada or a tranque). No federation text covers reaching the target in the middle of a hand. Fededodo publishes no rulebook that the researchers could find. Municipal Dominican tournaments: Santiago 2019 plays to 200 tantos, counts all tiles, and adds bonuses (pase de salida 25, capicua 25, paso corrido 0). La Guayiga 2025 has bonuses (capicua 30, paso corrido +30) but no counting basis in the claims. Neither tournament says whether a bonus can reach the target or whether a win can happen mid-hand.

synthesis.consensus:
Informal (patio) Dominican rules, one double-six set of 28 tiles. Every point below has at least two fetched Dominican sources, except where a point says otherwise.
(1) DEAL, 2v2 parejas. Partners sit across the table. Each player gets 7 tiles, so all 28 tiles are dealt. There is no pile and no drawing. Sources: DR1, Acento, DR1 forum, FichaFlow.
(2) DEAL, 1v1. Each player gets 7 tiles, and the other 14 stay face down in the pila. A player draws only when he has no legal move. He draws one tile at a time and stops at the first tile that fits. Wikipedia es says the player draws "una por una hasta encontrar aquella que pueda ser colocada". FichaFlow agrees on 7 tiles and a boneyard. No Dominican source says what happens when the pila is empty and the player still cannot play. The obvious rule is that he passes, and generic non-Dominican 1v1 games state it. A known Dominican variant deals 10 tiles each with no drawing (see variants).
(3) DIRECTION. Play goes counter-clockwise, so the next player is the one to the current player's right. Sources: DR1, Wikipedia es, FichaFlow, OurPastimes, DR1 forum, and FID agrees. For code, number the seats 0 to 3 in counter-clockwise order. Then next = (seat + 1) mod 4, and the teams are seats {0,2} and {1,3}. In 1v1 the turns alternate.
(4) FIRST HAND OF A MATCH. The holder of the 6-6 opens, and the opening tile must be the 6-6 itself (DR1, Wikipedia es, Santiago 2019 "SALIDA CON DOBLE SEIS", DR1 forum, El Inmobiliario, FichaFlow). In 2v2 the 6-6 is always in someone's hand, so the first opener is always known. The player who places the first tile is the "mano" for that hand (Acento). DR1 says this applies at the start of each match, so a rematch starts again with the 6-6.
(5) LATER HANDS, patio rule. The winner of the previous hand opens and may lead with any tile. The next player is to the opener's right. Sources: DR1, Wikipedia es, Acércate RD, La Mesa, FichaFlow (its most common rule), Boarden, Colonial Zone. The later hands have no forced double. In code, set the opener = the player who went out (domino). For a tranque, the sources do not name one player (see open questions).
(6) MUST PLAY. A player who holds a tile that fits either open end must play. He chooses which legal tile to play and on which end. He may pass only when no tile fits. Every source agrees: Wikipedia es, FichaFlow, La Mesa, the Santiago and La Guáyiga tournaments, FID, and USA Fed. A player who passes while holding a legal tile commits "pase con ficha", which is penalized (see federationView). In an app, the pass action must be impossible while a legal move exists. With that rule, the patio penalties never apply.
(7) SHUFFLE. A player of the losing team shuffles (Wikipedia es). This matters only for flavor text in the UI.
The main split between patio and tournament rules is item 5: tournaments rotate the opener instead.
synthesis.federationView:
International federations (not Dominican-specific, although FID 2015 lists Dominican delegates among its drafters):
- FID Reglamento (2015 Art. 74, 2024 Arts. 74 and 76): each player takes 7 tiles, and dealing and play go to the right (counter-clockwise). The first opener of a match is chosen by lot. Each player draws a tile, and the highest total opens, not the 6-6 holder. Each later hand is opened by the player to the right of the previous opener. This rotation ignores who won. Saying "paso" while holding a playable tile (Art. 81) brings a yellow card and a deduction of 40% of the target. If the false pass prevents a tranque or a domino, it brings a red card and loss of the match.
- FEMUNDO Reglamento 2025 (Arts. 6 and 8): 7 tiles per player. The first salida is drawn by lot, and after that it rotates. The shuffler is the player to the opener's left.
- USA Domino Federation: "La SALIDA es ROTATIVA". A false "paso" costs -25.
- No federation covers 1v1.
- The Dominican federation (Fededodo/FEDOMDOM) has no published rulebook online. The researchers found none.
Dominican municipal tournaments:
- Copa Alcaldía de Santiago 2019: the first hand opens with the 6-6, and after that the salida rotates. After a penalty or a tie, the player next in the rotation opens. A hand with five doubles is still played. A pase con ficha (and a "chivo", a tile that does not match) costs a 100-point swing: -50 for the offending pair and +50 for the other pair. Then the tiles are reshuffled.
- La Guáyiga 2025: a pase con ficha gives +30 to the opposing team. A tile the player lifts and commits must be played, which is a touched-tile rule. The tiles are reshuffled only when one player holds all 7 doubles.
Summary: tournaments and federations rotate the opener to the right each hand. Federations choose the first opener by lot, but the Dominican tournament uses the 6-6. The patio game gives the next lead to the winner.

synthesis.topic: Variants: other Dominican bonuses and customs (chuchazo, la caja, capicúa with a blank, pollona, dar agua, tournament vs informal rules, player expectations)
synthesis.consensus:
Implement two rule sets and let the table choose between them.

(A) FORMAL / "Regla General" (tournament mode). This follows FID 2024 and FEMUNDO 2025. The Dominican federation sends its national team to FEMUNDO events, so this is probably how its national events are played, but no Fededodo rulebook was found. In this mode there are NO bonuses: capicúa = 0, pase de salida = 0, pase corrido = 0, chuchazo = 0, and no shutout bonus. A hand ends only by dominada (a player goes out) or by tranque (the game is blocked). The hand score is the pips left in the players' hands. The match goes to the first pair that reaches or passes the target (200). Deal every hand as it falls. There is no redeal for many doubles (FEMUNDO Art. 5).

(B) INFORMAL / "Regla de Patio" (the default casual Dominican game). It adds the pase de salida, pase corrido and capicúa bonuses. The usual amount is 25 each, and some tables and the La Guáyiga tournament use 30. In DR1's version the pase de salida is 10 in games to 200 or 250 and 25 in games to 500. In patio play one table serves several pairs, and the losing pair gives up its seat.

The other items, one by one:

1) CHUCHAZO is not a Dominican bonus. It comes from Puerto Rico, where "la chucha" is the 0-0. There, going out with the 0-0 pays +100, but only in 500-point games. Default: 0, off. If you offer it, label it as a Puerto Rican option, never stack it with capicúa, and pay nothing in two cases: the 0-0 is the tile that causes a tranque, or the 0-0 closes two blank ends (Puerto Ricans call that "dominau"). A Dominican glossary uses "chuchazo" loosely for any hard blow, not for a tile.

2) LA CAJA is the Dominican name for the 0-0. Other names are "la cajita" and "el muerto", and the 6-6 is "el burro". The name carries no bonus. Use it only for tile names in the UI.

3) CAPICÚA WITH A BLANK: one Dominican source (the DR1 article) says a capicúa made with a blank does not count. No source pays extra for it. Default: treat it like any other capicúa. Offer "capicúa con blanco no vale" as a house-rule toggle, default off. Separately, all sources agree that a double closing both ends is NOT capicúa.

4) POLLONA is Cuban dictionary vocabulary for a shutout (losing without scoring a point). The Dominican word for a shutout win (for example 200-0) is "zapato", with the forms zapatero and zapatera; one Dominican scorekeeper app also shows "lisa". No reliable source gives a shutout point bonus in Dominican play. Show the shutout as a label or celebration only, with a bonus of 0.

5) DAR AGUA is a Cuban term, meaning the losing pair turns and mixes the tiles. The Dominican custom is the same act: a player of the losing team shuffles. The Dominican words for it are "barajar las fichas" or "lavar". In the app the shuffle is automatic. Only the wording matters, plus crediting the shuffle to the losing side if you animate it.

6) TOURNAMENT PENALTIES (a chivo, a tile that does not fit; passing with a playable tile; playing or opening out of turn) are for mistakes that the engine should make impossible. Enforce forced play: no pass while a legal move exists, and a tile picked up must be played. Then no penalty scoring is needed.

7) CUSTOMS a Dominican player recognizes: the teams are called "Largos" and "Cortos"; "manito" is the opener's partner after the opener makes the next opponent pass; "los mirones son de cera" means spectators stay silent; "juego en banda" is a hand where the tranque is forced; "dominar" means to win a hand; the loser shuffles; and the patio game uses winner-stays seating.
synthesis.federationView:
FID Reglamento 2024 (Art. 54: a hand ends only by dominada or by cierre/tranca) and FEMUNDO Reglamento de Competencia 2025 have no capicúa, pase de salida, pase corrido, chuchazo or shutout bonus. A hand scores only the tiles left. FID and FEMUNDO count every unplayed tile, including those held by the winner's partner. The match goes to the first pair that reaches the target (200). A tranque compares pair against pair. A tied tranque scores nothing, and the opener rotates. FEMUNDO Art. 5 says a hand is played with however many doubles a player draws, so there is no redeal. The FID 2015 drafters include Dominican delegates. Around 2010 the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico left the FID and founded the parallel FEMUNDO world championships. The Federación Dominicana de Dominó (Fededodo) ran a 14-match national championship in 2025 to pick its FEMUNDO team, but no Fededodo rulebook was found. FichaFlow calls the federation "FEDOMINO". One unreliable site says a "FEDOMDOM" cup uses double-nine tiles and a pollona penalty. Every other Dominican source describes double-six, so drop that claim.

Municipal Dominican tournaments are a mix. Copa Alcaldía de Santiago 2019 says it applies "reglas internacional", but it pays capicúa 25 and pase de salida 25 and pays nothing for the pase corrido. It plays sudden death (the losing pair leaves) and plays a hand even with five doubles. Passing with a playable tile swings 100 points (-50 to the offenders, +50 to the other pair), and then the tiles are redealt. A wrong opening gives 50 to the opponents. Its rule 6 ("con el de abajo") and rule 12 (pair against pair) contradict each other on the tranque. The La Guáyiga 2025 tournament pays capicúa 30 and lists "Paso corrido: +30 al equipo contrario", which is ambiguous. It gives +30 to the other team for a chivo, for playing out of turn and for opening out of turn. A tile picked up must be played. It redeals only if the 7 doubles come out. No federation or tournament source mentions chuchazo, la caja as a scoring event, capicúa with a blank, pollona or dar agua.

check.correctedConsensus:
The consensus holds in substance. Three corrections apply.

Keep the two rule sets.
(A) FORMAL / "Regla General" (tournament mode): no bonuses. FID 2024 is verified. Art. 54 says a hand ends only by dominada or by cierre/tranca, never by a penalty. Art. 57 and Art. 58 score all unplayed tiles, including the winner's own. A tranque goes to the pair with fewer pips. On a pip tie the tranque is a draw, and a zero is recorded to track future openings. Art. 61 plays World Championship matches to 200, with a 35-minute cap. Art. 62 gives the match to the first pair that reaches the target. The rulebook text has no capicúa, pase de salida, pase corrido, chuchazo or shutout bonus. The no-redeal rule (FEMUNDO Art. 5) was not checked in this pass.
(B) INFORMAL / "Regla de Patio": pase de salida, pase corrido and capicúa pay 25 or 30 each. Wikipedia (es) uses the two names "Regla General" and "Regla de Patio" literally and says Regla General is essentially the Latin game. In patio play the losing pair gives the table to the next pair, and a player of the losing team shuffles. Wikipedia does not state "three or more pairs" as a figure. Describe the patio setup as one table where the winner stays and the next pair waits.

Items 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7 stand as written. Chuchazo is Puerto Rican: the 0-0 is the chucha, it pays 100 only in 500-point games, it pays nothing on a tranque, and closing two blank ends is "dominau" (Mesa28 confirms all of this). A Dominican glossary uses "chuchazo" for a hard blow. "La caja" is the 0-0 and "el burro" is the 6-6, with no bonus attached. The loser shuffles ("barajar las fichas", or "lavar").

Correction 1 (item 3): the double rule. Wikipedia (es), Dominican section, explicitly says a double on the last play is not capicúa. The La Mesa glossary defines capicúa as going out with a tile that could close either end and says nothing about doubles. So replace "all sources agree" with "Wikipedia (es) and DR1 exclude doubles; the La Mesa glossary is silent." Remove the conflicting ownerView line that says "only La Mesa agrees", unless the La Mesa rules page (not opened here) supports it. The "capicúa con blanco no vale" toggle rests on DR1 alone. Wikipedia's capicúa text does not mention blanks.

Correction 2 (item 4): pollona. Pollona is not only Cuban vocabulary. The Dominican La Mesa glossary defines zapato as winning the match while the other pair has 0, and adds: "También se le dice pollona en algunas mesas." So the Dominican shutout labels are "zapato" (primary) and "pollona" (secondary, some tables). Zapatero/zapatera and "lisa" come from other apps not checked here. The bonus stays at 0. Show the shutout as a label or celebration only.

Correction 3 (wording): the consensus says Regla General "follows FID 2024 and FEMUNDO 2025". Wikipedia supports only "essentially the Latin game". The FID link is inferred, not stated by a Dominican source. The Fededodo-to-FEMUNDO link was not checked.

check.ownerViewCheck: Mostly holds, with two fixes. Holds: chuchazo is contradicted as a Dominican feature, because it is Puerto Rican (Mesa28) and Dominicans use the word for a hard blow (La Mesa). La caja is supported only as the tile name, with no bonus (Wikipedia). For dar agua, the word does not appear in Wikipedia or in the La Mesa glossary, while the custom (the losing team shuffles) is Dominican (Wikipedia). Fix 1: pollona is partly supported as Dominican vocabulary, not only Cuban. The La Mesa glossary says some Dominican tables call a zapato "pollona". It is still contradicted as a bonus, because no opened source pays points for it. Fix 2: the double-capicúa belief. Wikipedia (es) explicitly says a double is not capicúa, so that part of the contradiction is confirmed. The statement that "only La Mesa agrees" with the owner is not confirmed by the La Mesa glossary, which says nothing about doubles, and it conflicts with consensus item 3's "all sources agree". Keep one version: Wikipedia and DR1 exclude doubles, La Mesa's glossary is silent, and the La Mesa rules page was not checked. Capicúa with a blank is still thin support (DR1 only, not opened here).
